hero.title: Does he or she secretly love me?
hero.description: 10 questions about how they behave with you. We start by asking who you have in mind, so the questions talk about the right person.
hero.subtitle: Free, anonymous, instant result

howTo.title: How does it work?
howTo.step1: Think of one specific person before you start. A friend, a colleague, someone you run into often.
howTo.step2: You say whether it's a man or a woman, and the ten questions adapt.
howTo.step3: Answer on what you have actually observed, not on what you're hoping for.
howTo.step4: The result tells you whether these behaviours stand out or stay within the margin of friendship.
howTo.outro: The test is deliberately short. Beyond ten questions you start seeing signs everywhere, and that is exactly what to avoid.

crossLink.title: And what about you?
crossLink.text: If the real question is what you feel for this person, the other test is the one you want.

section1.title: What this test looks at, and what it cannot see
section1.p1: Someone behaves differently with you. You don't know whether it's in your head, whether it's friendship laid on a little thick, or whether that person simply doesn't dare say anything. And since you don't dare ask either, the situation can drag on for months.
section1.p2: This test doesn't read minds. It does something else: it compares what you have observed with what research on unspoken attraction looks at first. Some behaviours say a great deal, like the lingering look or the unusually precise memory. Others, like replying quickly to messages, mean almost nothing on their own.
section1.p3: The aim isn't to hand you a certainty, it's to spare you two symmetrical mistakes: seeing signs everywhere, or missing signals that, put end to end, form a fairly clear picture.

section2.title: The six signals that come up most
section2.intro: None of them is enough on its own. It's their accumulation, and above all the way they combine, that changes the reading.
section2.pillar1Title: The look that keeps coming back
section2.pillar1Text: The best documented signal. Not the sustained gaze, but the one you catch and that looks away. And its most telling variant: seeking your reaction after a joke, when the joke was for everyone.
section2.pillar2Title: A memory that is too precise
section2.pillar2Text: Remembering your cat's name, an exam you mentioned once, a series you hate. We retain effortlessly what concerns someone who matters. It's involuntary, and therefore hard to fake.
section2.pillar3Text: A lift offered when it isn't on the way, a coffee that lands exactly when you finish, a favour nobody needed. Once, that's kindness. Five times, that's a pattern.
section2.pillar4Title: Two behaviours depending on the audience
section2.pillar4Text: Much more open one to one, very neutral in a group. That contrast is one of the most reliable clues, because it gives away precisely what is being hidden: that something is going on.
section2.pillar5Title: The reaction when you mention someone else
section2.pillar5Text: A change of subject, a sudden silence, a criticism that doesn't sound like them. It isn't displayed jealousy, it's a reaction that escapes.
section2.pillar6Title: The circle that knows before you do
section2.pillar6Text: Sideways smiles, silence when you arrive, a friend who teases you. Those close by almost always know first, and they rarely keep a secret all the way.
section2.tip: An isolated signal says nothing. Someone who replies fast to your messages may reply fast to everyone. Always check whether the behaviour is reserved for you, or simply part of their character.

section3.title: What your score says
section3.p1: Each question carries a weight matching how serious it is, and each answer a value matching its rank. The total runs from 0 to 105 points. The four levels describe a probability, not a fact. Nobody, ourselves included, can know what someone feels without asking them.
section3.row1Analysis: The behaviour described doesn't stand out. It isn't a refusal, it's a snapshot.
section3.row2Analysis: Real signs, but all compatible with a fairly close friendship. Nothing settles the question.
section3.row3Analysis: Several strong signals in the same place. The interest goes beyond politeness, without being nameable.
section3.row4Analysis: The picture is hard to explain any other way. Probably only a conversation is missing.
section3.tip: A low score hurts more than a high one, and that's normal. But it says nothing about your chances: it describes what is happening today, not what could happen if you spoke.

section4.title: Attentive friendship or hidden feelings: where is the line?
section4.p1: That's the real difficulty. A very good friend easily ticks half this list: they remember things, they reply fast, they're glad to see you. The line doesn't run through the intensity of the attention, it runs through three details.
section4.sub1Text: Are they like that with you, or with everyone? A naturally warm person proves nothing. A reserved person who becomes talkative only with you is another matter.
section4.sub2Title: The gap between public and private
section4.sub2Text: This is the hardest sign to imitate. Friendship behaves the same in front of witnesses. A hidden feeling hides, so it changes face as soon as there are people around.
section4.sub3Title: What happens when a rival appears
section4.sub3Text: A friend is happy for you when you mention someone you like. Someone who was hoping for more reacts in a way that doesn't fit: too many questions, or none at all.

section5.title: Why people say nothing
section5.p1: If all the signals are there, one question remains: why not speak? The reasons are almost always the same, and none of them has to do with the strength of the feeling.
section5.sub1Title: Fear of losing what already exists
section5.sub1Text: By far the first one. When a friendship matters, declaring it means betting its existence on a single sentence. Many prefer a frustrating but stable situation to the risk of losing everything.
section5.sub2Text: Same team, same group of friends, same extended family. Speaking up involves far more than two people, and that prospect alone is enough to make someone back off.
section5.sub3Title: The belief that there's no chance
section5.sub3Text: The most frequent scenario, and the most absurd: two people each waiting for a sign from the other, and nobody moves. Both walk away thinking the feeling wasn't shared.
section5.tip: If you recognise yourself in those three paragraphs while thinking of yourself rather than the other person, the answer to your question may already be in the mirror.

section6.title: How to find out without breaking anything
section6.p1: You don't have to make a declaration. There are ways of opening the door without kicking it in, and they almost always produce an answer.
section6.sub1Title: Change the setting, not the speech
section6.sub1Text: A moment together that breaks your habits, an activity you've never done together, a slightly different context. Ambiguous signals become readable when the scenery changes, without anyone having to expose themselves.
section6.sub2Title: An open question rather than a declaration
section6.sub2Text: "I was wondering whether there was something else between us, or whether I was imagining it" doesn't stake your whole life and leaves both of you an honourable way out. It is far less risky than an "I love you" thrown out with no safety net.
section6.sub3Text: Many people can't answer on the spot, and hesitation isn't a no. What counts is what happens in the days that follow: the person comes back to you, or they pull away. Both are answers.
section6.tip: What to avoid: repeated indirect tests, ambiguous messages sent late at night, and asking a friend to sound them out for you. All of it eventually gets around and complicates exactly what you were trying to simplify.

section7.title: And if it's mutual?
section7.p1: Then you enter a phase that is pleasant and uncomfortable at once, where everything is possible and nothing is settled yet. Take your time: moving from friendship to something else requires adjustment, and stories that start this way are often among the most solid, precisely because they rest on years of knowing each other.
section7.p2: If you want to take stock of what is building, the am I in love test is about you directly, and the love compatibility test is taken together as soon as the situation is clear.
section7.p3: And if the answer is no, it doesn't undo what you were to each other. Plenty of friendships survive a declaration perfectly well, provided the one receiving the answer doesn't turn it into a grievance.
section7.tip: One last point, and it counts: someone's interest is not measured by your patience. If you have been waiting months for a sign that never comes, the absence of an answer is already one.

faq.q1: Can a test tell whether someone secretly loves you?
faq.a1: A test cannot know what someone feels. What it can do is compare the behaviours you describe with those that research on unspoken attraction observes most often, and tell you whether they stand out. The rest goes through a conversation, there is no other route.
faq.a2: Because beyond that, you start seeing signs everywhere. The ten kept here are the ones that best separate attentive friendship from a hidden feeling. Adding fifteen more wouldn't make the result truer, it would make it longer.
faq.q3: Does it work for someone who is already in a relationship?
faq.a3: The signals are the same, but the question changes completely. An interest that exists while someone is committed elsewhere puts everyone in a complicated position, and a high score is then not good news. Treat the result as information to handle with care.
faq.q4: My score is high but they still say nothing, why?
faq.a4: Almost always out of fear of losing what already exists. Speaking up means risking a friendship that matters, and many prefer a stable frustration to that risk. It is also why the first step often falls to whoever has the least to lose.
faq.q5: Should I take this test thinking of my partner?
faq.a5: No, it isn't designed for that. This test is for someone wondering about a person who hasn't spoken up: a friend, a colleague, an acquaintance. If you're already in a relationship with the person you have in mind, our couple tests answer your question far better.
faq.a6: No. Everything happens in your browser, nothing is sent or kept, and there is no account and no email address to give. You can retake the test as often as you like.
